cards.front: Which receptor does histamine use to switch on acid secretion by the parietal cell, and what does it do?
cards.back: H2 receptors on the basolateral membrane. Activation raises cAMP, which switches on the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump, the final step of acid secretion. Histamine is the dominant physiological stimulus; gastrin and acetylcholine act partly by releasing histamine from ECL cells.

cards.front: Why do H2 blockers also reduce acid responses to gastrin and acetylcholine?
cards.back: Histamine plays a permissive role. The cAMP made by H2 activation is needed for a full secretory response to gastrin and cholinergic agonists, so H2 blockade weakens the response to almost every secretagogue.

cards.front: Compare cimetidine, ranitidine and famotidine on potency and antiandrogen effects.
cards.back: Ranitidine is about 5 times as potent as cimetidine, and famotidine about 5 to 8 times as potent as ranitidine. Only cimetidine has antiandrogenic effects (gynaecomastia, loss of libido), raises prolactin and slows hepatic breakdown of estradiol. GG14 notes that some ranitidine and nizatidine preparations have been withdrawn because of contamination.

cards.front: Mechanism: omeprazole
cards.text: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the {{H+/K+ ATPase}} proton pump, and it is converted to its reactive form only in the acidic {{canaliculus}} of the parietal cell.

cards.front: Why are PPIs swallowed whole and taken before a meal?
cards.back: They are acid labile, so they are given as enteric-coated forms that must not be crushed or chewed. Taken on an empty stomach, the drug is in the blood when a meal switches the pumps on, and food lowers bioavailability.

cards.front: Why does a PPI take 3 to 4 days to reach full acid suppression?
cards.back: Each dose blocks only the pumps that are actively secreting, and the drug is cleared within 1 to 2 hours. Repeated dosing blocks more pumps until a plateau is reached at about 3 to 4 days, with 80 to 98 percent of 24-hour acid output suppressed. Secretion takes 3 to 4 days to return after stopping.

cards.front: What are the main concerns with long-term high-dose PPI therapy?
cards.back: Compensatory hypergastrinaemia with ECL-cell hyperplasia, fundic gland polyps and atrophic gastritis (tumour risk appears very low), and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping. Loss of the acid barrier raises the risk of infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia, community-acquired Clostridium difficile and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Reduced vitamin B12 absorption, hypomagnesaemia, and osteoporosis-related fractures are also reported, as are interstitial nephritis and, with omeprazole, gynaecomastia and erectile dysfunction.

cards.front: Why does omeprazole matter with clopidogrel, and which PPI has the fewest interactions?
cards.back: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, the enzyme that activates clopidogrel, which can blunt its antiplatelet effect. Omeprazole also raises levels of warfarin, diazepam and phenytoin. Pantoprazole has the lowest affinity for cytochrome P450 and the least interaction risk.

Why they have replaced H2 blockers as first-line acid suppressants

cards.front: Why is misoprostol seldom used for ulcers now?
cards.back: It is a synthetic PGE1 analogue that lowers acid output, but the effect lasts only about 3 hours, it relieves ulcer pain poorly, and it needs four times daily dosing. Diarrhoea, cramps and uterine bleeding are common, and it can cause abortion. Its main remaining role is preventing NSAID-induced ulcers.

cards.front: How does sucralfate protect an ulcer without neutralising acid?
cards.back: Below pH 4 it polymerises into a sticky gel that binds to the ulcer base and forms a physical shield against acid, pepsin and bile. It has no acid-neutralising action and is barely absorbed. Antacids must not be given with it, because they stop it polymerising.

cards.front: What is colloidal bismuth subcitrate, and why is it not an antacid?
cards.back: A colloidal bismuth compound that heals ulcers without raising gastric pH. It precipitates below pH 5. Its benefit may come from protecting the ulcer base, raising mucosal prostaglandin, mucus and bicarbonate, and acting directly on H. pylori. It causes black tongue and stools, and milk or antacids must be avoided with it.

cards.front: Why should every H. pylori-positive ulcer patient be offered eradication?
cards.back: Eradication is standard care in every H. pylori-positive gastric or duodenal ulcer: unless the patient keeps taking NSAIDs, it almost abolishes recurrence. H. pylori also drives chronic gastritis and contributes to gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric MALT lymphoma, which can regress after eradication. KDT adds that where testing is unavailable, failed or relapsing ulcers should still receive eradication therapy.

cards.front: Which H. pylori eradication regimens are listed in the textbooks?
cards.back: GG14 (newest): triple therapy for 10 to 14 days, a PPI twice daily with clarithromycin 500 mg and amoxicillin 1 g twice daily (metronidazole 500 mg can replace amoxicillin); bismuth quadruple therapy for 10 to 14 days, a PPI with bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole four times daily; sequential therapy (PPI + amoxicillin for 5 days, then PPI + clarithromycin + tinidazole or metronidazole for 5 days); or PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin for 10 days. Where resistance to clarithromycin and metronidazole is common, a 14-day quadruple regimen is advised. KDT cites the older US-FDA regimen: lansoprazole 30 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily for 2 weeks (86 to 92 percent eradication).

Linked to gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma
A PPI raises gastric pH and enhances amoxicillin and clarithromycin activity
Amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole or tinidazole, tetracycline, levofloxacin
Bismuth: active against H. pylori and resistance does not develop to it
Single antibiotics fail and breed resistance; use two or three antibiotics with a PPI
10 to 14 days is better than shorter courses (GG14); KDT notes 1-week triple therapy gives about 85 percent

Triple: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole) twice daily
Bismuth quadruple: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole for 10 to 14 days, used first where resistance is high and for treatment failures
Alternatives: sequential therapy; PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin
Recent nitroimidazole use: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin
Recent macrolide use: PPI + metronidazole or tinidazole + amoxicillin

Sucralfate, bismuth and misoprostol as protectives

Bleeding ulcer: high-dose IV PPI, then oral PPI

cards.front: Classify: ulcer protectives
cards.text: {{Sucralfate}} forms a protective gel below pH {{4}}, and {{misoprostol}} is a synthetic {{PGE1}} analogue that lowers acid output.

cards.front: H. pylori regimen after a recent macrolide
cards.text: After recent macrolide use, the H. pylori regimen is a PPI with amoxicillin and {{metronidazole}} or {{tinidazole}}, and {{clarithromycin}} is left out.

Magnesium salts: laxative; accumulate in renal failure
Aluminium hydroxide: constipating, binds phosphate, toxicity in renal failure

cards.front: Short note: Drug therapy of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

points: Lower oesophageal sphincter tone is the main barrier
Fats, alcohol, smoking, anticholinergics, nitrates and calcium channel blockers lower LES tone
Acid is the key aggressive factor

Stage 2 and 3: PPI, often twice daily, usually long term
PPI: most effective; heals 80 to 90 percent of lesions in 4 to 8 weeks
H2 blocker: mild disease; healing in 50 to 70 percent
Alginate: floating raft over gastric contents, no effect on LES
Prokinetics: adjuncts only, weaker than acid suppression
Light early dinner, raised head of bed, weight loss, avoid triggers

cards.front: Classify: antacid salts
cards.text: Magnesium hydroxide is {{fast-acting}} and laxative, aluminium hydroxide is {{slow-acting}} and {{constipating}}, so combining them balances the effect on the bowel.

cards.front: Where is the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and why can blood-borne drugs act on it?
cards.back: In the area postrema, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so circulating drugs, toxins and hormones can act on it directly. It relays signals to the nucleus tractus solitarius, which drives the vomiting centre in the medulla.

cards.front: How do cytotoxic drugs and radiation trigger vomiting through serotonin?
cards.back: Gut cell damage releases 5-HT from enterochromaffin cells. It activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents, which carry the signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius and the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Substance P acting on NK1 receptors adds to the signal.

cards.front: What is an effective IV ondansetron schedule for highly emetogenic cisplatin?
cards.back: KDT: 8 mg IV given slowly over about 15 minutes, starting about 30 minutes before the cisplatin infusion, then two more 8 mg doses 4 hours apart; a single 24 mg dose on day 1 has also been used, and 8 mg orally twice daily for 3 to 5 days for delayed vomiting. GG14 gives the adult dose as 8 to 16 mg IV or 16 to 24 mg orally. Ondansetron alone is weak against delayed vomiting, so it is combined with dexamethasone and an NK1 antagonist.

cards.front: Why is palonosetron preferred for delayed chemotherapy-induced vomiting?
cards.back: It has the highest 5-HT3 receptor affinity and the longest half-life in its class (about 40 hours), so it controls delayed vomiting (days 2 to 5) better than ondansetron and keeps its efficacy in repeat cycles. Dose: 250 microgram (0.25 mg) by slow IV injection 30 minutes before chemotherapy, not repeated within 7 days. GG14 notes that, unlike first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists, it does not appear to prolong the QT interval.

cards.front: What does aprepitant add to a standard antiemetic regimen, and what are its key interactions?
cards.back: It is a selective NK1 antagonist that blocks substance P in the brain. Added to ondansetron and dexamethasone for cisplatin, it mainly improves protection against delayed vomiting. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so it can raise dexamethasone levels and alter warfarin effect, and those doses need adjusting.

cards.front: Which receptors does metoclopramide use in the gut to speed gastric emptying?
cards.back: It is a 5-HT4 agonist on myenteric neurones, which increases acetylcholine release and so improves propulsive contraction and lower oesophageal sphincter tone. Its D2 blockade in the gut and weak 5-HT3 block add to this at higher doses. Atropine blocks the 5-HT4 effect.

cards.front: What are the adverse effects of metoclopramide, and which are most important in children?
cards.back: Sedation, dizziness, loose stools and extrapyramidal effects: acute dystonias (more common in children and young adults, often after IV use and possibly after a single dose) and parkinsonism after weeks of use. Tardive dyskinesia can follow chronic use and may be irreversible. Hyperprolactinaemia causes galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia; QT prolongation and methaemoglobinaemia in neonates are also reported.

cards.front: How does domperidone differ from metoclopramide?
cards.back: Domperidone is a D2 antagonist that barely crosses the blood-brain barrier, so extrapyramidal effects are rare and it does not oppose levodopa in Parkinson disease. Its prokinetic action is not reversed by atropine. It still acts on brain areas outside the barrier: the chemoreceptor trigger zone (antiemetic) and prolactin control (galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia). It carries a risk of serious ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, especially above 60 years and at doses over 30 mg/day.

cards.front: Why was cisapride withdrawn from most markets?
cards.back: It blocks cardiac delayed-rectifier potassium channels, which prolongs the QT interval and risks torsades de pointes. The risk rises with CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals and macrolides. It was banned in India in 2011.

cards.front: Which antiemetic class is first choice for motion sickness, and when should it be taken?
cards.back: Drugs with anticholinergic and antihistaminic action: hyoscine (the most effective, but short acting, so suited to short journeys) and H1 antihistamines such as promethazine, dimenhydrinate and meclozine. They work best when taken about 1 hour before the journey. Dopamine blockers and 5-HT3 antagonists are less effective.

cards.front: Metoclopramide: receptor actions
cards.text: Metoclopramide acts as a {{5-HT4}} agonist in the gut and as a {{D2}} antagonist in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

cards.front: Classify: dopamine-blocking antiemetics
cards.text: Phenothiazines such as {{prochlorperazine}} and butyrophenones such as {{haloperidol}} block {{D2}} receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

cards.front: Classify: CINV drugs
cards.text: The NK1 antagonist {{aprepitant}} blocks the action of {{substance P}}, while the 5-HT3 antagonist {{ondansetron}} blocks {{5-HT}} signals on vagal afferents.

cards.front: Ursodiol and gallstones
cards.text: Ursodiol dissolves small cholesterol gallstones by {{lowering}} the cholesterol content of bile; its plasma half-life is about {{4 days}} because of enterohepatic cycling.

cards.front: Why must bulk-forming laxatives be taken with plenty of water, and what do they not do?
cards.back: They swell by absorbing water, which softens stool and speeds transit. Without enough fluid they can cause impaction, and ispaghula must never be swallowed dry. They take several days for full effect and do not soften stool already in the rectum, so they prevent constipation rather than treat it.

cards.front: Why are stimulant laxatives such as bisacodyl and senna contraindicated in pregnancy and in bowel obstruction?
cards.back: They can stimulate the gravid uterus reflexly, and they increase propulsion and fluid secretion, which is dangerous with an obstruction. Regular use causes hypokalaemia and colonic atony, and senna can cause melanosis of the colon.

cards.front: How does lactulose lower blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.back: Colonic bacteria break lactulose down into acidic, osmotically active products. The lower stool pH turns ammonia into the ionised, non-absorbable ammonium form, and the laxative effect clears it. Blood ammonia can fall by 25 to 50 percent. Lactitol works similarly.

cards.front: What are prucalopride and lubiprostone, and what is the key safety point for each?
cards.back: Prucalopride is a 5-HT4 agonist that boosts colonic propulsion. It is used for chronic constipation in women when other laxatives fail, and appears to lack the cardiovascular risk that ended tegaserod. Lubiprostone is a prostaglandin analogue that opens chloride channels to draw fluid into the gut; nausea is its commonest side effect, and it is reserved for patients who have failed at least two other laxative classes.

cards.front: What are the components and total osmolarity of the WHO low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution?
cards.back: Sodium 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, potassium 20 mmol/L, chloride 65 mmol/L and citrate 10 mmol/L, with a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L. The older standard formula (310 mOsm/L, higher sodium) caused periorbital oedema in children and produced more stool and vomiting.

cards.front: What is the role of zinc in acute childhood diarrhoea, and how is it given?
cards.back: Given with low-osmolarity ORS, zinc shortens and reduces the severity of the episode and lowers recurrence for 2 to 3 months. It is given for 10 to 14 days: 20 mg per day for children aged 6 to 60 months and 10 mg per day under 6 months.

cards.front: Why does loperamide cause few central effects, and when must it be avoided?
cards.back: It is a peripheral mu-opioid agonist (40 to 50 times as potent as morphine as an antidiarrhoeal) that is poorly absorbed and barely enters the brain, so at normal doses it has no analgesic action and little abuse liability. GG14 warns that exceeding the recommended dose can cause torsades de pointes, cardiac arrest and death. Avoid it in invasive diarrhoea (fever, blood or mucus; risk of toxic megacolon and systemic spread), in severe colitis, and in young children (KDT: under 4 years; GG14: not recommended under 2 years).

cards.front: How does racecadotril reduce diarrhoea without slowing the gut?
cards.back: It is a prodrug converted to thiorphan, an enkephalinase inhibitor. By protecting natural enkephalins it lowers mucosal cAMP and cuts intestinal secretion, but leaves motility alone. It is not contraindicated in children; the usual dose is 100 mg three times daily for up to 7 days.

cards.front: In acute diarrhoea, which features suggest an invasive cause that needs an antibiotic?
cards.back: Blood and mucus in the stool, fever, urgency and cramps, with only mild dehydration, point to colonic invasion (for example Shigella, EPEC, Campylobacter or Salmonella typhimurium). Watery diarrhoea with vomiting and little fever points to a noninvasive cause, where oral rehydration is the mainstay.

cards.front: Short note: Classification of laxatives

points: Laxative: soft formed stool; purgative: stronger, more fluid evacuation
Ispaghula, methylcellulose, bran: water-holding, fermentable fibre
Docusate: anionic detergent that draws water into stool
Liquid paraffin: lubricant; avoid regular use (granulomas, lipid pneumonia, fat-soluble vitamin loss)
Bisacodyl and sodium picosulfate: act on colonic mucosa and enteric neurones
Senna and cascara: anthraquinone glycosides activated by colonic bacteria; act in 6 to 8 hours
Magnesium and sodium salts: bowel preparation, poisoning, tapeworm clearance
Lactulose and lactitol: fermented to acidic osmotic products
Prucalopride (5-HT4 agonist), lubiprostone (chloride channel activator)

cards.front: Short note: Constipation, rational treatment and purgative abuse

points: A symptom: infrequent hard stool, straining or incomplete evacuation
Normal frequency varies from once every 2 days to 3 times daily
Functional: spastic (hard stool, irritable bowel) or atonic (age, debility, laxative abuse)
Secondary: obstruction, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, opioids, anticholinergics, oral iron, clonidine, verapamil
Diet, fluids, exercise and regular habits first
Spastic: soluble fibre; atonic: bulk or osmotic agent; stimulants last
Enema preferred to treat impaction
Keep stool soft in hernia, cardiovascular disease and perianal surgery
Bowel preparation: saline purgative, bisacodyl or senna
Hypokalaemia, steatorrhoea, protein-losing enteropathy, spastic colitis

cards.front: Short note: Management of acute infectious diarrhoea

Most acute diarrhoea is self-limiting
Oral route for mild to moderate loss
IV if loss exceeds 10 percent of body weight, stool loss exceeds 10 ml per kg per hour, or oral intake is impossible
Ringer lactate or a sodium, potassium and bicarbonate solution as IV fluid
Do not starve; continue breast milk, rice, banana, soup and fruit juice
Noninvasive: no routine antibiotic
Invasive: ciprofloxacin or another fluoroquinolone, cotrimoxazole or doxycycline (KDT); fluoroquinolones are first line for traveller's diarrhoea in adults (GG14)
Cholera: tetracycline halves stool volume
C. difficile: stop the offending antibiotic; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are now preferred, metronidazole only for nonsevere disease
Avoid antibiotics in enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (haemolytic uraemic syndrome)
Zinc in children; probiotics have weak evidence for routine use

cards.front: Short note: Antidiarrhoeal drugs

Racecadotril: enkephalinase inhibitor

Octreotide: somatostatin analogue for carcinoid or VIP tumour diarrhoea; given subcutaneously
Loperamide: potent peripheral opioid, most suitable antimotility drug for adults
Diphenoxylate with atropine: CNS effects; contraindicated under 6 years
Codeine: not used for diarrhoea because of dependence
Avoid antimotility drugs in invasive diarrhoea, severe colitis and young children

cards.front: Essay: Drug therapy of inflammatory bowel disease

points: Ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal disease of the colon, spreading up from the rectum
Crohn's disease: patchy transmural disease anywhere in the gut
Extraintestinal features in up to half of patients
Sulfasalazine: releases 5-ASA in the colon; sulfapyridine causes most side effects; give folic acid
Mesalazine, olsalazine, balsalazide: deliver 5-ASA to the colon with fewer side effects; 5-ASA not useful in Crohn's
Prednisolone to induce remission, then taper; not for long-term maintenance
Budesonide (delayed-release) targets ileal or colonic disease with fewer systemic effects
Azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine for steroid-dependent or resistant disease; check TPMT status
Methotrexate for severe Crohn's disease, given parenterally
Cyclosporine as a short bridge in severe ulcerative colitis
Anti-TNF: infliximab (closes fistulas; better with azathioprine) or adalimumab for moderate to severe disease
Vedolizumab: blocks lymphocyte homing to gut mucosa (MAdCAM-1 binding); Crohn disease and UC
Ustekinumab: anti-IL-12/IL-23 (p40); Crohn disease
Tofacitinib: oral JAK inhibitor

cards.front: Essay: Oral rehydration therapy in acute diarrhoea

points: Sodium absorption coupled to glucose by the sodium-glucose cotransporter survives in diarrhoea
Secreted fluid contains no glucose, so it cannot be reabsorbed
Isotonic or slightly hypotonic: osmolarity 200 to 310 mOsm/L
Glucose equal to or slightly above sodium, not above 110 mM
Potassium 15 to 25 mM and a base such as citrate 8 to 12 mM
WHO low-osmolarity formula: 245 mOsm/L; less stool output and vomiting than the older formula
Frequent drinks; replace stool losses; aim to restore hydration within about 6 hours
Nasogastric drip if a weak child refuses
ORS does not stop diarrhoea; zinc is added in children; food should not be withheld

cards.front: Sulfasalazine: how it works
cards.text: Colonic bacteria split the {{azo}} bond of sulfasalazine to release {{5-aminosalicylic acid}}, the active anti-inflammatory part, and {{sulfapyridine}}, which causes most side effects.

cards.front: Azathioprine: a dangerous genetic interaction
cards.text: Azathioprine is converted to {{6-mercaptopurine}}; patients deficient in the enzyme {{TPMT}} are at high risk of severe bone marrow toxicity.

cards.front: Diphenoxylate: classification and limits
cards.text: Diphenoxylate is a synthetic {{opioid}} given with {{atropine}} to discourage abuse, and it is contraindicated below {{6}} years of age.

cards.front: Short note: Prebiotics and probiotics in bowel disorders

points: Probiotics are live microbes such as lactobacilli, bifidobacteria and Saccharomyces boulardii
Prebiotics are poorly digested fibres or oligosaccharides that feed beneficial gut bacteria
Synbiotics combine both
Some strains shorten acute infectious diarrhoea in children
Saccharomyces boulardii and Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea
Probiotics aid H. pylori eradication by improving response to antibiotics
Probiotics help prevent the first attack and relapse of pouchitis
